title: Activities
text:
The Bag Game
image

Resources
An opaque (cloth) bag, a tray of pinecones or other similar objects.


Details
Part 1: The children sit in a ring. Show them the empty bag. The bag is passed around the ring with each child adding one pinecone in turn. They count along as each pinecone is added. Before reaching 10 cones in the bag, stop the count, and ask if we know how many cones are in the bag altogether. They may wish to demonstrate the amount using their fingers. After discussion, tip out to check. Repeat, starting again with the empty bag.
Part 2: As above, but start by counting 6 cones into the bag together. Pass the bag of 6 cones around the ring, with each child removing one cone, counting backwards until the bag is empty.


What to say

How many are there altogether in the bag? Can you show me using your fingers?
How many are in the bag now? How do we know?
Fin said “Three”, so what does Salim say now?
Let’s count back as we take them out, together.



What matters

Understanding the cardinality principle involves knowing that the last number you say establishes the quantity of the whole group. Asking “How many are in the bag now’, and “How many are there altogether in the bag?” before tipping out the bag to check draws children’s attention to the last number said.
The items can be changed but must be similar in both type and colour to aid counting of the whole group.
Counting back is as important as counting forwards, but children are not as confident with this and might need to become familiar with the practicalities of the game (one at a time, taking turns) in order to focus on what number to say.

title: Activities
text:
Did you know that…
… understanding the directional property of the counting list is a core insight in early number learning?
What is the directional property of the counting list?
Children need to grasp that each number in the counting list represents a quantity that is one more than the one before, and one less than the one after. The “bag game” is useful because it focuses directly on this idea. Children add or remove objects from a bag and have to work out how the total changes.


More…

Unlike many counting activities, where children count objects they can see, this task does not allow them to rely only on pointing and saying number words. In some counting tasks, children can succeed by following a routine of matching each object to a number word without fully understanding how counting works (Gelman & Gallistel, 1978; Sarnecka & Carey, 2008). In contrast, the bag game requires them to think about how the quantity changes when one item is added or taken away.
The activity can be easily adapted to suit different levels. When small numbers are used (up to three or four), children may be able to keep track of the objects mentally without counting. However, with larger numbers, this is no longer possible. At that point, children need to use their knowledge of counting to work out the new total, moving forwards or backwards in the counting list (Carey, 2009; Piazza et al., 2010).
Research shows that even children who can count may not yet understand how numbers change when one is added or removed (Sella & Lucangeli, 2020; Sarnecka & Carey, 2008). This activity helps to reveal and develop that understanding. Overall, the bag game supports children in moving beyond simply reciting numbers, helping them understand how numbers are ordered and connected (Carey & Barner, 2019). This is an important foundation for later arithmetic.
